alloys.name: Aluminium 1100-H14 (1100-O for contrast)
alloys.family: 1xxx commercially pure aluminium (99.0% Al min), non-heat-treatable, strengthened only by cold work (H tempers)
alloys.heat_limit_c: Cannot over-age (no precipitation hardening). The H14 strength comes from cold work, which fades progressively when heated (recovery, then recrystallisation to the O temper); no tube-specific temperature found. 1100-O is already fully soft: typical yield only 35 MPa, UTS 90 MPa, 35% elongation.
alloys.heated_hazards: Bare metal gives off no meaningful fume at a few hundred C: aluminium melts about 660 C (NIOSH lists 1220 F) and boils far higher. Fine dust from sanding or cutting is combustible. Paint, tape or plastic on the tube can smoke; that is the coating, not the metal.
alloys.corrosion: Kaiser rating A (best) general and stress-corrosion
alloys.tube_availability: Kaiser makes 1100-O extruded seamless tube and lists cold-drawn specs (ASTM B210, AMS 4062); the alloy is 'subject to cast lot quantity restriction'. Retail stock in 5/8-1 in OD was not checked. Not a structural staff tube in practice.
alloys.staff_verdict: Not recommended for fire or contact staffs. H14 yield is about 42% of 6061-T6 and O temper is about 13%, so it bends easily. Its only plus is the highest thermal conductivity of the list. OK only for a throwaway LED or prop tube.
alloys.notes: Values are Kaiser typical values (0.0625 in specimen). Thermal conductivity 222 W/m-K is for O temper; H18 is 218.

alloys.notes: Kaiser typical values: H14 is 22 ksi UTS and 21 ksi yield; O is 16 ksi UTS and 6 ksi yield.

alloys.name: Aluminium 6061-T6 (drawn tube)
alloys.family: 6xxx Al-Mg-Si, heat-treatable, solution treated and artificially aged (peak aged)
alloys.heat_limit_c: Over-ageing, meaning permanent loss of room-temperature yield, depends on both time and temperature. Read by eye from MMPDS-04 Fig. 3.6.2.2.1(d), so the numbers are approximate: loss starts at about 120 C (250 F) after 10,000 h, about 150 C (300 F) after 1,000 h, and about 190 C (375 F) after 1/2 h. After 1/2 h at about 260 C (500 F), roughly two-thirds of the T6 yield remains. Long exposures at or above about 230-260 C bottom out near 20% of the T6 yield, which is about the O-temper 55 MPa. While hot, strength at about 150 C is roughly 70-85% of room-temperature yield (MMPDS Fig. 3.6.2.2.1(b)).
alloys.heated_hazards: No meaningful fume from the bare or anodized tube at a few hundred C. Cutting or sanding dust is a combustible-dust hazard. Hazards come from coatings, grips and tape near the wick, not from the alloy.
alloys.corrosion: Kaiser rating B general, A stress-corrosion for T6
alloys.tube_availability: The most available staff tube. Drawn seamless tube is made to ASTM B210/B483 and AMS 4080-4083, with Kaiser walls from 0.018 to 0.250 in. Online Metals lists 3/4 in OD x 0.058 in wall drawn T6. Speedy Metals lists 3/4 in x 0.065 in wall. Fire Mecca sells hard-anodized drawn 6061-T6 in 3/4 in and 7/8 in OD, which telescope. The drawn T6 spec minimum is 290 MPa UTS and 241 MPa yield, with 10% elongation for 0.025-0.049 in walls and 12% for 0.050-0.259 in walls (full section).
alloys.price_note: Checked 2026-09-24: Speedy Metals 3/4 in OD x 0.065 in wall, 72 in length, $11.51. Fire Mecca hard-anodized 6061-T6 staff tubing, $6.67 per ft (about $40 for 6 ft). Online Metals refused automated access, so its price was not captured.
alloys.staff_verdict: The baseline. Cheap, everywhere, anodizes well, and forgiving: it bends before it breaks and can usually be straightened (Kaiser cold-workability rating C). Downsides: about half the yield of 7075-T6, so it bends more easily on hard drops. Like every T6 temper, it can slowly lose temper at the wick ends if the metal there runs hot for long cumulative times. Fine for LED and practice staffs; a solid budget fire staff.
alloys.notes: Typical values: Kaiser 0.0625 in specimen. Spec minimums: Kaiser drawn tube table and MMPDS Table 3.6.2.0(c1), where the A-basis drawn T6 values are 42 ksi Ftu and 35 ksi Fty.

alloys.name: Aluminium 6063-T6
alloys.family: 6xxx Al-Mg-Si, solution treated and artificially aged
alloys.heat_limit_c: Peak-aged Mg-Si alloy, so the over-ageing behaviour should be similar to 6061-T6 (inference). The Maljaars/TNO study reports that EN 1999-1-2 includes 6063-T6 reduction factors for exposures up to 2 h.

alloys.staff_verdict: About 78% of the 6061-T6 yield, with better corrosion resistance and anodize finish. Acceptable for LED or practice staffs; 6061-T6 or 7075 are better for fire contact staffs.

alloys.name: Aluminium 6063-T832 (drawn tube temper)

alloys.name: Aluminium 7075-T6
alloys.family: 7xxx Al-Zn-Mg-Cu (5.1-6.1% Zn, 2.1-2.9% Mg, 1.2-2.0% Cu), peak aged
alloys.melting_c: 477-635 C (Aluminum Association typical via MatWeb and Alcoa: solidus 890 F). Kaiser's tube sheet gives 532-635 C.
alloys.heated_hazards: No fume from the solid tube at staff temperatures. The zinc (about 5.6%) boils at 907 C, far above the alloy's melting range, so zinc oxide fume (the cause of metal fume fever) needs melting, welding or torch-cutting. The dust caveat applies as for the other grades.
alloys.heat_limit_c: T6 is aged at only about 120 C for 24 h, lower than 6061. The over-aged T73 temper is made by holding at about 160-180 C for 24 h or more. So many cumulative hours in that range drift a T6 tube toward T73 strength, about 14% lower yield, and hotter or longer exposure keeps going down. The annealing temperature is 413 C. No 7075 residual-strength curve was obtained; that is the next check.
alloys.corrosion: Kaiser: general C and stress-corrosion C for T6, the worst here apart from 2024. Anodize or keep dry.
alloys.tube_availability: Drawn seamless tube is made in O, T6, T73 and T76 (Kaiser; ASTM B210, AMS-WW-T-700/7). Online Metals lists 7075-T6 drawn tube, but it was not fetched. Flow-arts sellers: Dark Monk 19 x 1.4 mm (about 3/4 in), also 16, 22 and 25 mm; buyfirefans 19.1 x 1.4 mm x 1.62 m; the Matrix staff (Threeworlds, AU) uses 22 mm extruded 7075. general_findings: STIFFNESS IS THE SAME FOR EVERY ALUMINIUM ALLOY. Kaiser gives elastic modulus 68.3-73.1 GPa across 1100, 3003, 5052, 6061, 6063, 2024, 7050 and 7075, and densities run 2.68-2.85 g/cc. For the same OD and wall, every alloy flexes and whips almost identically and weighs within about 5%. The alloy only changes how much bending the tube survives before it takes a permanent set (yield), plus corrosion and heat behaviour. To change flex, change OD or wall, not alloy.

MY OWN CALCULATION (no source): for a 3/4 in OD x 0.058 in wall tube, section modulus is about 332 mm3. The bending moment to start a permanent bend (typical yield x section modulus) is about 48 N-m for 6063-T5, 92 for 6061-T6, 90 for 6063-T832, 96 for 6082-T6, 144 for 7075-T73, 167 for 7075-T6 and 227 for 7068. Mass of a bare 5 ft (1.524 m) tube: about 335 g in 6061 at 0.058 in wall, about 371 g at 0.065 in wall, and about 331 g for 19 x 1.4 mm 7075. Recompute before quoting.

OVER-AGEING IS TIME x TEMPERATURE, AND CUMULATIVE. MMPDS-04 Fig. 3.6.2.2.1(d) plots the room-temperature yield of 6061-T6 after exposures of 1/2 h to 10,000 h. Read by eye (approximate): loss begins at about 120 C for 10,000 h, about 150 C for 1,000 h and about 190 C for 1/2 h. After 1/2 h at about 260 C, roughly 2/3 of the yield remains. Long exposures above about 230-260 C bottom out near 20% of T6 yield (about the O temper). Nobody has published the metal temperature under a burning wick, so whether a staff crosses these lines is unknown. If the tube just under the wick reaches 200-300 C for about 5 minutes per burn, a few dozen burns could add up to hours at that temperature. That is an inference, not a measurement. A cheap check: temperature-indicating crayons or labels on the metal next to the wick.

Maljaars (TNO/TU Eindhoven, 2005) literature study on aluminium in fire (https://pure.tue.nl/ws/files/2310557/633114.pdf): artificially aged tempers (T5-T8) lose strength as temperature rises. Naturally aged tempers (T1-T4) can first gain strength from artificial ageing, turning at about 200 C for 0.5-1 h. Cold-worked (H) tempers lose their cold-work strength. 'In general, the largest reduction in the 0,2 % proof stress occurs between 100 °C and 350 °C.' It also notes that EN 1999-1-2 tabulates proof-strength reduction factors for exposures up to 2 h.

UNVERIFIED, DO NOT QUOTE WITHOUT CHECKING THE STANDARD: a search-engine summary claimed these EN 1999-1-2:2023 Table 5.1 proof-strength factors (at 100/150/200/250/300 C, up to 2 h exposure): 6061-T6 0.95/0.91/0.79/0.55/0.31; 6063-T6 0.91/0.84/0.71/0.38/0.19; 6082-T6 0.90/0.79/0.65/0.38/0.20; 5052-H34 1.00/0.92/0.52/0.29/0.20. I could not open the standard text. The 2005 Maljaars study says the edition of the time used 1.0 at 100 C for all alloys, so the numbers may differ between editions.

MELTING: the lowest incipient-melting points are in the 7xxx and 2xxx alloys: 7075 about 477 C (Alcoa solidus 890 F), 7068 about 476 C, 2024 about 502 C. 6061 is about 582 C, 6082 about 555 C (Aalco), and 1100/3003 about 640 C. All are well above a 'few hundred C' tube temperature, but a bare tube section held in a flame (for example a wick burned down to the metal) could approach them. Structural strength is effectively gone long before melting.

FUMES: at staff temperatures, bare or anodized aluminium gives off no meaningful fume. NIOSH lists aluminium melting at 1220 F (660 C) and boiling at 4221 F. The zinc in 7xxx alloys (4-8%) boils at 907 C (Wikipedia, zinc), above the alloys' melting range, so zinc oxide fume (metal fume fever; NIOSH lists chills, muscle ache, nausea, fever, cough) needs melting, welding or torch-cutting. The realistic hazards: (1) fine sanding or cutting dust. OSHA: 'Even materials that do not burn in larger pieces (such as aluminum or iron)' can explode as dust, and NIOSH says 'finely divided dust is easily ignited'. (2) Coatings, paint, grip tape, heat-shrink or glue near the wick smoking. That is inference; check what the finish is. Aerospace tube can carry chromate conversion coatings, which can contain hexavalent chromium; I did not verify this for any listed product.

OUT-OF-SCOPE WARNING, verify with the steel researcher: the Flow Arts Institute suggests hardware-store 'conduit' as a cheap practice staff. Much EMT conduit is zinc-galvanized STEEL, not aluminium, and heating the zinc coating near a wick is a different fume question from aluminium.

WHAT FLOW-ARTS MAKERS USE (checked 2026-09-24): Dark Monk uses 7075-T6 (19 x 1.4 mm, 72 in; staffs 55-67 in, 3/4 in OD). The Matrix contact fire staff (Threeworlds AU) uses 22 mm anodised extruded 7075, 680 g at 1400 mm. Fire Mecca sells hard-anodized drawn 6061-T6, 3/4 and 7/8 in OD, which telescope. buyfirefans sells 7075-T6 19.1 x 1.4 mm. The Flow Arts Institute says '6061 or 7075 being the standard'. A search snippet (page not loadable, HTTP 503) said LMF Props upgraded to 7075-T6. I did not verify any UK or Australian maker using 6082 or 6063.

MAKER STATEMENTS ON HEAT: the Threeworlds Matrix page says aluminium is flame and heat proof but 'gets very hot where it is close to the flame'. Dark Monk says silicone wraps near the wicks are 'the difference in grabbing a hot coffee mug vs a hot cast iron pan'. Neither gives a temperature.
SIZING: Dark Monk's rule is 'measure from the ground to just above your chin'; it sells 55-67 in lengths and says experienced spinners may prefer longer or shorter. A 5-6 ft tube covers most adults.

COMMON WALLS near 3/4 in OD in US stock: 0.035, 0.049, 0.058 and 0.065 in (Aircraft Spruce 2024-T3 list; Online Metals 6061-T6 at 0.058; Speedy Metals 6061-T6 at 0.065). Flow-arts 7075 is typically 1.4 mm (0.055 in). Kaiser draws walls from 0.018 to 0.250 in. Dark Monk notes thicker walls add weight and slow spin but resist bending, and heavier staffs suit beginners.

STRAIGHTNESS: the Aluminum Association standard tolerance for drawn tube 0.375-5.999 in OD (reprinted by Kaiser, Table 12.25) is 0.010 in per foot of measured length, about 0.06 in over 6 ft. Extruded tube is the same (Table 12.8). Tolerances do not apply to O temper.

STRAIGHTENING A BENT STAFF: Kaiser rates cold workability for 6061-T6 and 6063-T6 as C and for 7075-T6/T73 and 7068 as D. Dark Monk says 7075 'can be cold formed some, but not much. It cracks.' Expect to be able to bend a 6061 staff back sometimes; a bent 7075 staff may crack instead.

CORROSION RANKING (Kaiser general / stress-corrosion ratings): 1100, 3003, 5052 and 6063 A; 6061 B; 7075-T6 C/C; 7075-T73 C/B; 7050 C/B; 7068 C/C; 2024 D. For a staff that sees sweat, rain or salt, anodized 6xxx is the low-maintenance choice.

THERMAL CONDUCTIVITY ranges from about 120 W/m-K (2024) and 130 (7075-T6) to 167 (6061-T6), about 200 (6063) and 222 (1100). Inference, not measured on staffs: a more conductive tube pulls heat away from the wick zone faster, lowering peak metal temperature there but warming more of the tube toward the hands.

MARKETING CLAIMS TO CORRECT: 'strongest aluminum commercially available' for 7075-T6 (Dark Monk, buyfirefans) is not true; Kaiser's 7068-T6511 has 683 MPa typical yield vs 503. 'Equivalent to titanium' depends entirely on which titanium grade; see the titanium research. '7075 is 2x 6061' holds for typical yield (503 vs 276 MPa, about 1.8x).

SCANDIUM-ALUMINIUM ('Scandium' bikes, bats, tent poles, lacrosse shafts): Wikipedia says 'These alloys contain between 0.1% and 0.5% of scandium' and that titanium alloys are cheaper and more widely used. A bicycle maker (IBEX, 2006 forum post) called scandium frames aluminium 'alloyed with a small amount of Scandium' and too expensive for the general market. They are proprietary, usually butted or shaped bike tubes, and I found no straight round tube for sale or published tube properties. I gave them no numeric entry rather than invent values. Not relevant for staff builders.

SIX-SIX vs SEVEN-OH: the drawn temper 6063-T832 has spec minimums (283/248 MPa for thin walls) practically equal to 6061-T6 drawn (290/241 MPa). If a stockist sells it, it is an equal-strength alternative with better corrosion resistance and anodize.

DATA-SOURCE CAVEATS: MatWeb, ASM (asm.matweb.com), Online Metals, Metals Depot and Metals4U refused automated access (403 or refused), and the web-search budget ran out mid-task. Typical values therefore come from Kaiser Aluminum tube datasheets (Rev. 05/06 and KA-TPH 1.09), Alcoa's 7075 sheet, Aalco (UK), a 2006 MatWeb printout of Aluminum Association typical data, and MMPDS-04 (2008). Kaiser's drawn-tube limit table prints the MPa columns swapped for 7075-T6 and T73 (77 ksi is 531 MPa, not 455). Typical values are not design minimums. All prices were looked at on 2026-09-24.
